title: Switchable giant room-temperature nonlinear Hall effect in Bilayer Graphene
authors: Margherita Melegari, Ignacio Gutiérrez-Lezama, Justin C. W. Song, Alberto F. Morpurgo
abstract: Utilizing quantum second-order nonlinear transport for practical junction-free devices require materials with large and tunable nonlinearites at room temperature -- a current materials platform challenge. Here, we report the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in double-ionic gated bilayer graphene devices that enable unusually strong inversion breaking. We observe NLHE that are readily switchable (on, off, and sign reversed) with second order nonlinear susceptibilities $χ^{(2)}_{yxx}$ that reaches giant room-temperature values of $3\,10^{-3}\,μ\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{S/V}$, comparable to values commonly observed at low temperature in WTe$_2$ or in graphene-based moiré superlattices, and three-to-four orders of magnitude larger than values reported in material systems recently employed in search of a room-temperature NLHE. Our devices produce corresponding THz voltage responsivities $\simeq 4\,10^{4}\,\mathrm{V/W}$, comparable to commercially available Schottky diodes. These are orders of magnitude better than for previously reported room-temperature NLHE devices rendering double-ionic gated bilayer graphene a choice platform for junction-free nonlinear technology.
summary: This work reports observing a giant and switchable nonlinear Hall effect in double-ionic gated bilayer graphene at room temperature. By utilizing the ionic gating to break inversion symmetry, the authors achieved nonlinear susceptibilities significantly larger than previously reported room-temperature values. This positions bilayer graphene as a promising platform for next-generation, junction-free nonlinear electronic technology.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing materials with large and tunable nonlinearities at room temperature for practical, junction-free electronic devices.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a switchable, giant nonlinear Hall effect in double-ionic gated bilayer graphene, achieving susceptibilities comparable to low-temperature records.
method: Measurements involved injecting alternating current at a fixed frequency and measuring both the second harmonic ($2\omega$) and fundamental ($\omega$) transverse and longitudinal voltages while sweeping gate voltages.
model_or_system: The study uses double-ionic gated Bernal stacked bilayer graphene (BLG) devices. The ionic gating allows for precise control over the perpendicular electric field ($E_{BLG}$), which is crucial for breaking inversion symmetry.
key_observables: Nonlinear Hall voltage ($V_{2\omega}^{xy}$), second-order nonlinear susceptibility ($\chi^{(2)}_{yxx}$), and THz voltage responsivity.
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, perpendicular electric field strength ($E_{BLG}$), and the magnitude of $\chi^{(2)}_{yxx}$ ($\sim 3 	imes 10^{-3} \mu	ext{m S/V}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed nonlinear response is dominated by the second-order susceptibility and that the ionic gating mechanism provides the necessary symmetry breaking.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, the dependence of longitudinal resistance on gate voltages, and the sign change of the nonlinear transverse voltage ($V_{2\omega}^{xy}$) upon reversing the perpendicular electric field.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the measurement setup, confirms the nonlinear Hall effect's dependence on the perpendicular electric field, rules out trivial contributions (like the Berry curvature dipole), and quantifies the resulting large nonlinear coefficients.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer large, switchable nonlinear responses at room temperature in a 2D material platform like graphene is highly relevant for developing novel quantum electronic components that operate outside cryogenic conditions.
